title: The painted cloth
hookLine: a mural goes up, and nobody looks at the wall
carry: brahman is the cloth under every figure
tomorrow: ten cross a river, nine reach the bank. or do they?
last: THE WORLD GIVEN, THE WORLD LAID OVER.

cards: The art club has been on the hallway wall all week, painting the graduation mural. First they scrubbed it. Then a coat of primer.
Then pencil lines, faint as breath. Now the colors: a skyline, a river, a crowd of faces in caps and gowns. Students stop between classes to find themselves in it.
Nobody stops to look at the wall. An old book of Advaita verses watches a painter do the same thing, with a cloth, and asks a strange question. Where did the cloth go?

teach.b: The book is the Panchadashi, and this chapter is called the lamp of the picture. It follows the painter step by step. A clean cloth.
The cloth stiffened with starch. Outlines drawn. Colors filled in.

The clean cloth, the book says, is like pure awareness, Brahman, and each later step adds a layer, until the whole crowded scene of the world appears. The cloth never leaves. Every hill and face sits on it the whole time.
Then the chapter catches a detail that's easy to miss, and it's the one worth telling someone tonight.
The painted people wear painted clothes, and those clothes are painted to look like cloth. A viewer could take the painted cloth for the real one underneath.

In the same way, the book says, each person has a borrowed glow of awareness, reflected in the mind, and takes it for the awareness behind everything. Many teachers read that borrowed glow as the small I, the ego.
That's the knot. Not the painting. Paintings are lovely.
The mistake is losing track of what it's painted on.

teach.h: LOOK TWICE: THE SCENE AND THE CLOTH.
teach.b: So the chapter asks for a way of looking twice: enjoy the scene, and know the cloth. Nobody has to scrub off the mural to see the wall.

teach.h: THE CLOTH IS UNDER EVERY FIGURE.
teach.b: That's Advaita's big claim: Brahman, the one reality, is under everything, and under you. Tradition credits the book to Vidyaranya, a teacher in Shankara's line. Other Hindu schools read the self differently.

how: Students of Advaita may read the Panchadashi with a teacher, a chapter at a time, talking through each picture before going on.

a book of hymns sung at dawn in the Vedas
a book of rules for temple worship and festivals

games.q: a friend starts reading Advaita and says, 'so the world is fake and nothing matters.' what does the painted cloth say?
o: the painting is fine to enjoy; the mistake is forgetting the cloth, Brahman, under it.
right: the picture is fake, so scrub it off and ignore it.
the picture is all there is; there's no cloth underneath.
games.why: the chapter never asks anyone to scrub off the painting. look twice: enjoy the scene, know the cloth.

practice: Find one picture near you: a poster, a photo, the pattern on a mug. Rest your eyes on it for the sit, and let the image be the image.
Every so often, notice the surface it sits on, the paper, the glass, the wall, there the whole time.

wordCard.voice: The Panchadashi: a book of Advaita verses. Here, the one that stands before a painted world and asks after the cloth.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a picture; the chapter is the Chitradipa, the lamp of the picture.

carryVoice: For the road: Brahman is the cloth under every figure, the whole time. Three days into this book.

sources.ref: Panchadashi 6.1–7 and following (Chitradipa: the cloth washed, starched, outlined and colored as an image of the self and its layers; painted figures wearing painted clothes like the cloth, as reflected consciousness mistaken for the real)
